description:
Wesam Saad opens the church chapter by distinguishing the universal church from a local congregation. Everyone bought by Christ and born again belongs to Christ’s body, regardless of nationality or denominational label. This shared life creates a real bond between believers, but it does not remove the particular responsibilities of a local church with its own leaders, members and gathered worship.

The command to make disciples in Matthew 28 gives local churches a common purpose. Wesam argues that congregations should therefore help one another advance the gospel, rather than regard their own success as sufficient. He points to churches supporting the Jerusalem believers and to practical help between like-minded congregations, including providing preaching when another church has a need.

The discussion then examines the command to regard one another as more important than oneself. Loving Christians elsewhere cannot substitute for loving the people of one’s own congregation. Yet that local commitment is no permission for indifference towards others. Humility and selflessness developed in the church should overflow into wider relationships. The session closes by leaving a further question for discussion: can someone belong to Christ’s universal body while refusing commitment to a local church?

questions.question: Who belongs to the universal church?
questions.answer: The study identifies its members as people bought by Jesus Christ and born again. Nationality or a denominational label does not settle that question; genuine believers share the same spiritual life under Christ, who is the head.

questions.question: How does a local church differ from the universal church?
questions.answer: A local church has a particular congregation, leadership and responsibilities. Its people gather to worship and use their gifts to build up that body. The universal church describes the wider body of Christ rather than one congregation under its own elders.

questions.question: Why should local churches help other congregations?
questions.answer: They share the command to make disciples of all nations. Wesam reasons that a congregation should not be satisfied with its own progress while another struggles, when it has an opportunity to provide help for the sake of the gospel.

questions.question: What kinds of cooperation does the session describe?
questions.answer: It recalls the Macedonian churches collecting support for Jerusalem and describes building relationships with like-minded churches. In the local example, ministers may fill a preaching need elsewhere, making sacrifices so another congregation can be strengthened.

questions.question: Why is loving Christians elsewhere no replacement for serving one’s own congregation?
questions.answer: Wesam stresses the particular people addressed by the command to regard one another as more important. Helping others can be good, but neglecting the members to whom one is already committed leaves that local responsibility unfulfilled.

questions.question: Does a special responsibility to the local church justify indifference towards other believers?
questions.answer: No. The teacher explicitly rejects that conclusion. Genuine humility and selflessness cannot simply be left behind when a person meets Christians elsewhere. The local church is where that character is deliberately exercised, and it should also affect wider relationships.

questions.question: What question is left for the following discussion?
questions.answer: Wesam asks whether enjoying Christian friendships within the universal church is sufficient if a person refuses to join a local church. He presents that objection for further discussion rather than completing its answer in this recording.

questions.question: What remains uncertain in the discussion about church life in the age to come?
questions.answer: Wesam does not identify a definite future structure corresponding to present local churches. He acknowledges the limits of what he can establish from Scripture and treats suggestions about how future learning and responsibilities might be arranged as uncertain.
